people.name: Cathy Freeman
people.why: Lit the Olympic flame and won the 400 m in Sydney in 2000, carrying both the Australian and Aboriginal flags.

people.name: Howard Florey
people.why: Turned penicillin from a curiosity into a usable drug, saving more lives than almost anyone in history.

people.name: Sidney Nolan
people.why: His Ned Kelly series is the defining image of the Australian outback in art.

people.name: Don Bradman
people.why: A career batting average of 99.94, a statistical outlier unmatched in any sport.

people.name: Eddie Mabo
people.why: His case overturned the legal fiction that Australia was empty land before 1788.

events.title: First peoples arrive
events.what: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have the longest continuous cultures on earth.

events.title: The First Fleet
events.what: Britain founded a penal colony at Sydney Cove, beginning dispossession that is still being reckoned with.

events.title: Federation
events.what: Six colonies became one country, with a constitution and a still-unresolved relationship to the Crown.

events.title: Mabo
events.what: The High Court recognised native title, ending terra nullius as a legal doctrine.

events.title: The Apology
events.what: Parliament apologised to the Stolen Generations of Aboriginal children removed from their families.

culture.label: Outdoors
culture.text: Most Australians live within an hour of the coast, and the beach is a shared public space rather than a resort.

culture.label: Sport
culture.text: Four football codes plus cricket. Which one dominates depends entirely on which state you're in.

culture.label: Humour
culture.text: Dry, self-deprecating and heavy on teasing. Being sent up is usually a sign you're accepted.

culture.label: Coffee
culture.text: The flat white is an Australian (or New Zealand) invention, and café standards are unreasonably high.

culture.label: Art
culture.text: Aboriginal art from the Western Desert is the country's most significant contribution to world art.

talkAbout: Which city or state they're from — the rivalries are constant and cheerful.
Coffee, and their opinion of it wherever they've travelled.
The outdoors: surfing, bushwalking or whatever gets them out of the house.
avoid: Aboriginal dispossession, deaths in custody and Australia Day are live political arguments, not conversation openers. Don't do the accent.

people.name: Edmund Hillary
people.why: With Tenzing Norgay, the first to summit Everest, in 1953 — and a beekeeper by trade.

people.name: Kate Sheppard
people.why: Led the campaign that made New Zealand the first country to give women the vote, in 1893.

people.name: Ernest Rutherford
people.why: Split the atom and discovered the nucleus; the father of nuclear physics.

people.name: Whina Cooper
people.why: Led the 1975 land march the length of the North Island at the age of 79.

people.name: Jonah Lomu
people.why: Changed what a winger could be, and made rugby a global spectacle at the 1995 World Cup.

events.title: Māori settlement
events.what: Polynesian voyagers navigated to Aotearoa by star, swell and bird, the last major landmass humans reached.

events.title: Treaty of Waitangi
events.what: Signed between the Crown and Māori chiefs; its Māori and English texts differ, and that difference still shapes the country.

events.title: Women's suffrage
events.what: The first self-governing country in the world where women could vote in national elections.

events.title: Nuclear-free
events.what: New Zealand banned nuclear ships, losing its US alliance and gaining an identity.

culture.label: Greeting
culture.text: The hongi presses noses and foreheads together, sharing breath. Kia ora is used by everyone.

culture.label: Rugby
culture.text: The All Blacks are close to a national institution, and the haka before a match is not a gimmick.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: A hāngī cooks food in an earth oven over hot stones — the centre of a Māori gathering.

culture.label: Te reo
culture.text: Māori is an official language, taught in schools and increasingly heard in everyday speech and broadcasting.

culture.label: Outdoors
culture.text: 'Tramping' is hiking, and the hut network makes multi-day walks genuinely accessible.

talkAbout: The outdoors, and which walks or islands they rate.
Rugby, but also netball and cricket.
Te reo Māori — asking how to pronounce a place name properly is welcome.
avoid: Don't call them Australians, and don't assume Australia and New Zealand are interchangeable. Treaty settlements and Māori-Crown relations are political, so listen first.

people.name: Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna
people.why: Oxford-educated chief who shaped modern Fijian institutions and land law.

people.name: Vijay Singh
people.why: Three major championships and a spell as world number one, from Lautoka.

people.name: Seru Epenisa Cakobau
people.why: Unified much of Fiji and ceded it to Britain in 1874 to escape debt and war.

people.name: Waisale Serevi
people.why: Widely regarded as the greatest sevens player who ever lived.

people.name: Epeli Hau'ofa
people.why: His essay 'Our Sea of Islands' reframed the Pacific as vast and connected, not small and isolated.

events.title: Cession to Britain
events.what: Fiji became a Crown colony after Cakobau ceded sovereignty.

events.title: Indentured labour
events.what: About 60,000 workers came from India to the sugar plantations; their descendants are now roughly a third of Fiji.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Fiji became independent after 96 years of British rule.

events.title: Olympic gold
events.what: Fiji won its first ever Olympic medal — gold, in rugby sevens — and the country stopped for a week.

culture.label: Kava
culture.text: Yaqona, made from pounded pepper root, is drunk in a formal circle; accepting a cup is how you join the group.

culture.label: Sport
culture.text: Rugby sevens is the national obsession, and Fiji are perennial world champions at it.

culture.label: Village life
culture.text: Land is held communally by clans, and most Indigenous Fijians belong to a village even if they live in town.

culture.label: Sevusevu
culture.text: Visitors present a gift of kava to the village chief before staying — a genuine protocol, not a show.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Lovo is an earth-oven feast; Indo-Fijian curries are equally part of everyday eating.

talkAbout: Rugby sevens, and the 2016 gold.
Which island or province their family is from.
Kava, and the etiquette of the circle.
avoid: Relations between Indigenous Fijians and Indo-Fijians, and the coups of 1987, 2000 and 2006, are sensitive. Modest dress matters in villages.

people.name: Michael Somare
people.why: Led Papua New Guinea to independence in 1975 and is called the father of the nation.

people.name: Mekere Morauta
people.why: Rebuilt state institutions and the central bank after a period of collapse.

people.name: Dame Carol Kidu
people.why: For years the only woman in parliament, and the leading voice on women's and children's rights.

people.name: Ryan Pini
people.why: Commonwealth champion and the country's most successful swimmer, a five-time Olympian.

people.name: Mathias Kauage
people.why: Self-taught painter whose bold contemporary work brought Papua New Guinean art to the world.

events.title: The highlands 'discovered'
events.what: Australian prospectors found a million people living in valleys outsiders had assumed were empty.

events.title: The Kokoda campaign
events.what: Some of the Pacific War's hardest fighting, and the reason Kokoda means so much to Australians too.

events.title: Independence
events.what: PNG became independent from Australian administration.

events.title: The Bougainville conflict
events.what: A war over a copper mine killed thousands; Bougainville voted overwhelmingly for independence in 2019.

culture.label: Language
culture.text: Over 800 languages — more than any other country, roughly a tenth of all the languages on earth.

culture.label: Sing-sing
culture.text: Clans gather in feathers, shells and paint to perform; the Goroka show draws a hundred groups.

culture.label: Pigs
culture.text: Pigs are wealth, bride price and obligation, not just food.

culture.label: Sport
culture.text: Rugby league is the national sport and the closest thing to a unifying passion.

culture.label: Wantok
culture.text: The wantok system — obligation to those who speak your language — is the real social safety net.

talkAbout: Which province and language group they come from.
Rugby league, and the State of Origin series.
The sing-sing festivals and what each group's decoration means.
avoid: Bougainville and 'tribal fighting' are complex and often sensationalised abroad; ask rather than assume. Sorcery accusations and violence against women are real problems, not curiosities.

people.name: Walter Lini
people.why: An Anglican priest who led Vanuatu to independence in 1980 and coined 'Melanesian socialism'.

people.name: Grace Mera Molisa
people.why: Vanuatu's best-known writer, whose poetry attacked the exclusion of women from public life.

people.name: Hilda Lini
people.why: One of the first women elected to parliament and a long-standing campaigner for a nuclear-free Pacific.

people.name: Chief Roi Mata
people.why: His burial site is Vanuatu's only World Heritage listing, and his peace-making is still recounted.

people.name: Marie-Noëlle Ferrieux Patterson
people.why: As the country's first Ombudsman she published reports naming corruption at the top of government.

events.title: The Condominium
events.what: Britain and France governed jointly in an arrangement so absurd it was nicknamed the Pandemonium — two police forces, two legal systems.

events.title: Cargo cults
events.what: Wartime American supply drops gave rise to movements like John Frum on Tanna, still observed today.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Vanuatu became independent, immediately putting down a secession attempt on Espiritu Santo.

events.title: Cyclone Pam
events.what: A category five storm damaged or destroyed most buildings in the country and made Vanuatu a leading voice on climate loss and damage.

culture.label: Land diving
culture.text: On Pentecost, men dive from wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles — the ritual that inspired bungee jumping.

culture.label: Kava
culture.text: Vanuatu's kava is the strongest in the Pacific, drunk at dusk in a nakamal in near silence.

culture.label: Language
culture.text: More languages per head of population than anywhere on earth — over 100 for 300,000 people.

culture.label: Kastom
culture.text: Kastom means traditional law and practice, and it runs alongside the formal legal system.

culture.label: Wellbeing
culture.text: Vanuatu has repeatedly topped the Happy Planet Index, which locals enjoy pointing out.

talkAbout: Which island they're from — the differences are enormous.
Kava, and how Vanuatu's compares to Fiji's.
Climate change: they have been at the front of the international argument.
avoid: Don't treat kastom or the John Frum movement as quaint. Cyclones and rising seas are lived experience, not a talking point.

people.name: Peter Kenilorea
people.why: The country's first prime minister at independence in 1978.

people.name: Jacob Vouza
people.why: Captured and bayoneted by Japanese troops on Guadalcanal, he escaped and delivered his warning; knighted for it.

people.name: Sir Frank Kabui
people.why: Led the country's legal system and then the state through the post-conflict years.

people.name: Rennie Fugui
people.why: A star of the Kurukuru, the national futsal side that has dominated Oceania.

people.name: Celsus Talifilu
people.why: A prominent voice in the debate over the country's foreign alignments and provincial autonomy.

events.title: Guadalcanal
events.what: The turning point of the Pacific War; wrecks still lie in Iron Bottom Sound.

events.title: Independence
events.what: The Solomon Islands left British protection.

events.title: The Tensions
events.what: Ethnic conflict between Guale and Malaitan communities brought the state close to collapse.

events.title: RAMSI
events.what: An Australian-led regional mission restored order and stayed fourteen years.

culture.label: Shell money
culture.text: Strings of polished shell discs are still made on Malaita and used for bride price and compensation.

culture.label: Sea
culture.text: Almost a thousand islands; boats do the work roads do elsewhere.

culture.label: Panpipes
culture.text: 'Are'are bamboo panpipe ensembles are among the most distinctive music in the Pacific.

culture.label: Language
culture.text: Around 70 languages, with Solomon Islands Pijin as the shared tongue.

culture.label: Wantok
culture.text: As in PNG, obligation to your language group organises much of daily life.

talkAbout: Which island and language group they belong to.
Diving and the wartime wrecks, which draw visitors from everywhere.
Futsal and football — the Kurukuru are a genuine source of pride.
avoid: The Tensions are recent and unresolved for many families. The country's shifting relations with China and Taiwan are politically charged.

people.name: Albert Wendt
people.why: The founding figure of modern Pacific literature in English.

people.name: Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III
people.why: Shot dead by New Zealand police during a peaceful independence march on Black Saturday.

people.name: Fiame Naomi Mata'afa
people.why: Samoa's first woman prime minister, who took office in 2021 after a constitutional standoff.

people.name: Manu Samoa's 1991 side
people.why: Beat Wales in Cardiff at their first World Cup, and announced Pacific rugby to the world.

people.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
people.why: Spent his last years at Vailima, took the name Tusitala — teller of tales — and is buried on Mount Vaea.

events.title: Partition
events.what: Germany and the United States divided the archipelago, creating Samoa and American Samoa.

events.title: The influenza catastrophe
events.what: A ship allowed to dock brought flu that killed about a fifth of the population in weeks.

events.title: Black Saturday
events.what: New Zealand police fired on a peaceful Mau demonstration, killing eleven including Tamasese.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Samoa became the first Pacific island nation to gain independence in the twentieth century.

culture.label: Fa'a Samoa
culture.text: 'The Samoan way' — the matai chief system, extended family and church organise nearly everything.

culture.label: Tatau
culture.text: The pe'a and malu are hand-tapped tattoos taking days to complete; tattoo itself is a Samoan word.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Umu cooking over hot stones above ground, and palusami — taro leaves baked in coconut cream.

culture.label: Sport
culture.text: Samoa produces professional rugby players far out of proportion to its size.

culture.label: Sunday
culture.text: Sunday is genuinely observed: church, a large lunch, and very little else.

talkAbout: Family and village — the first question a Samoan asks is usually where you're from.
Rugby, and Samoan players in overseas leagues.
Tatau, and what the designs mean.
avoid: Don't confuse Samoa with American Samoa. Respect Sunday and village curfew for evening prayers; dress modestly away from resorts.

people.name: Queen Sālote Tupou III
people.why: Reigned 47 years and won over Britain by riding through the 1953 coronation rain in an open carriage.

people.name: Tāufa'āhau Tupou I
people.why: United the islands, abolished serfdom and gave Tonga a constitution in 1875.

people.name: Pita Taufatofua
people.why: Competed at both summer and winter Olympics, and carried the flag oiled and bare-chested.

people.name: Epeli Hau'ofa
people.why: Tongan-raised thinker whose work reframed how the Pacific sees itself.

people.name: 'Akilisi Pōhiva
people.why: Campaigned for decades for democratic reform and became the first commoner prime minister.

events.title: The kingdom united
events.what: Tāufa'āhau took the name George Tupou I and brought the islands under one crown.

events.title: The constitution
events.what: Tonga's founding law helped it stay the only Pacific nation never formally colonised.

events.title: Democratic reform
events.what: The king gave up most executive power to an elected parliament.

events.title: Hunga Tonga eruption
events.what: The largest volcanic explosion in over a century sent a tsunami across the Pacific and cut the country's only cable.

culture.label: Monarchy
culture.text: The last Polynesian kingdom, and never formally colonised — a point of considerable pride.

culture.label: Ta'ovala
culture.text: A woven mat worn around the waist for formal occasions, over Western clothes.

culture.label: Sport
culture.text: Rugby is close to a national identity; the sipi tau is Tonga's pre-match challenge.

culture.label: Whales
culture.text: Humpbacks calve in Tongan waters, and it is one of the few places you can legally swim with them.

culture.label: Sunday
culture.text: The constitution makes Sunday sacred: trade and work are prohibited by law.

talkAbout: That Tonga was never colonised.
Rugby, and Tongan players abroad.
Whale season and the islands' geography.
avoid: Criticism of the royal family lands badly. Sunday restrictions are law, not custom — plan around them.

people.name: Toaripi Lauti
people.why: Tuvalu's first prime minister after separating from the Gilbert Islands.

people.name: Simon Kofe
people.why: Delivered a speech to COP26 standing knee-deep in the sea, an image that travelled the world.

people.name: Etimoni Timuani
people.why: Tuvalu's sole athlete at the 2016 Olympics, carrying the flag alone.

people.name: Sir Tomasi Puapua
people.why: A doctor who led the country through the 1980s and later represented the Crown.

people.name: Kausea Natano
people.why: Led Tuvalu's push for a legal framework preserving statehood even if the land goes under.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Tuvalu separated from the Gilbert Islands and left British rule.

events.title: Selling .tv
events.what: Leasing its internet domain to broadcasters became a major share of national revenue.

events.title: The COP26 speech
events.what: Simon Kofe addressed the summit standing in the sea where there had been dry land.

events.title: The Falepili Union
events.what: A treaty with Australia offering Tuvaluans residence as the sea rises — a first of its kind.

culture.label: Elevation
culture.text: The highest point is about 4.6 m. Tuvalu is among the countries most exposed to sea-level rise anywhere.

culture.label: Falekaupule
culture.text: The island council of elders makes decisions collectively; central government works with it, not over it.

culture.label: Fatele
culture.text: Sung and danced in rows on a mat, speeding up as it goes, at every celebration.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Fish, coconut and pulaka, a swamp taro grown in dug pits — increasingly threatened by salt water.

culture.label: Scale
culture.text: About 11,000 people. Everyone is related to everyone, and reputation travels instantly.

talkAbout: The .tv domain, which they find funny and useful in equal measure.
Fatele dancing and island celebrations.
How a country of 11,000 punches above its weight at the UN.
avoid: Don't treat Tuvalu as a doomed curiosity — 'the country that will disappear' is a framing many find dehumanising. Ask what they want the response to be.

people.name: Ieremia Tabai
people.why: Became Kiribati's first president at 29 and led it for twelve years.

people.name: Anote Tong
people.why: Made Kiribati the global face of climate displacement and bought land in Fiji as insurance.

people.name: David Katoatau
people.why: Danced after every lift at the Olympics to get the world's attention on rising seas.

people.name: Teburoro Tito
people.why: Led the country for a decade and later served as its ambassador to the UN.

people.name: Sister Alaima Talu
people.why: Wrote the first history of Kiribati by an I-Kiribati author.

events.title: The phosphate years
events.what: Banaba was strip-mined for fertiliser until the island was ruined and its people resettled in Fiji.

events.title: The Battle of Tarawa
events.what: Seventy-six hours of fighting killed over 6,000 people on an atoll of a few square kilometres.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Kiribati left British rule; its 33 atolls straddle the equator and the date line.

events.title: Moving the date line
events.what: Kiribati shifted the line so the whole country shared one day — and gained the world's earliest sunrise.

culture.label: Scale
culture.text: Land the size of a small city, spread across an ocean area bigger than India.

culture.label: Dance
culture.text: Kiribati dance is famously still — the arms and eyes carry it, and the bird-like head movement is the signature.

culture.label: Maneaba
culture.text: The village meeting house, where seating position reflects clan and every decision is made.

culture.label: Food
culture.text: Fish, coconut, breadfruit and babai — the pit-grown giant taro reserved for feasts.

culture.label: Time
culture.text: Kiribati's Line Islands are the first place on earth to see each new day.

talkAbout: Being first into the new year, every year.
Traditional dance, and why the stillness is the difficult part.
Ocean and fisheries — Kiribati manages one of the world's biggest marine reserves.
avoid: As with Tuvalu, the 'sinking nation' framing grates. Banaba's mining and resettlement remain a live grievance.

people.name: Tosiwo Nakayama
people.why: The first president of the Federated States, who held four very different island groups together.

people.name: Manny Mori
people.why: An accountant who led the country for eight years and pushed its climate diplomacy.

people.name: Emelihter Kihleng
people.why: The first Pohnpeian to publish a collection of poetry in English.

people.name: Isaac Figir
people.why: A long-serving legislator central to the renegotiation of the Compact with the United States.

people.name: Dr. Eliuel Pretrick
people.why: Built the national health system almost from scratch over four decades.

events.title: Nan Madol built
events.what: A city of 90 artificial islets built from basalt logs on a reef off Pohnpei — the Venice of the Pacific.

events.title: Operation Hailstone
events.what: The US attack on the Japanese fleet at Chuuk sank dozens of ships now famous among divers.

events.title: Independence
events.what: The Federated States became sovereign under a Compact of Free Association with the United States.

events.title: Compact renewed
events.what: The agreement covering funding, defence and free movement to the US was extended for twenty years.

culture.label: Yap stone money
culture.text: Limestone discs up to four metres across, quarried in Palau; ownership changes without the stone moving.

culture.label: Diversity
culture.text: Four states — Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei, Kosrae — with different languages and customs, across 2,700 km.

culture.label: Sakau
culture.text: Pohnpei's kava, pounded on a stone and drunk from a coconut shell in near silence.

culture.label: Diving
culture.text: Chuuk Lagoon holds the largest concentration of shipwrecks on earth.

culture.label: Reciprocity
culture.text: Giving and returning food and goods is how status and obligation are managed.

talkAbout: Which of the four states they're from — they'll expect the distinction.
Nan Madol, and how it was built.
Diving, and the lagoon.
avoid: Don't call it 'Micronesia' without care — that's the region, and Guam, Palau and the Marshalls are separate. The Compact and migration to the US are debated.

people.name: Haruo Remeliik
people.why: Palau's first president, assassinated in office during the nuclear-free constitution struggle.

people.name: Tommy Remengesau Jr.
people.why: Created one of the world's largest marine sanctuaries, closing 80% of Palau's waters to fishing.

people.name: Bilung Gloria Salii
people.why: One of the highest-ranking women in Palau's matrilineal chiefly system.

people.name: Ibedul Yutaka Gibbons
people.why: Led opposition to nuclear-armed ship visits over more than a decade of referendums.

people.name: Surangel Whipps Jr.
people.why: A prominent international advocate for ocean protection and small-island climate action.

events.title: The Battle of Peleliu
events.what: Expected to take four days, it took over two months and cost around 12,000 lives.

events.title: The nuclear-free constitution
events.what: Palau adopted the world's first constitution banning nuclear weapons, then held eight referendums over it.

events.title: Independence
events.what: The last UN trust territory became sovereign, in free association with the United States.

events.title: The Palau Pledge
events.what: Every visitor must sign a promise, stamped in their passport, to protect the islands.

culture.label: Ocean
culture.text: The Rock Islands are World Heritage-listed, and Jellyfish Lake holds millions of stingless jellyfish.

culture.label: Matrilineal
culture.text: Clan land and titles pass through women, and senior women choose the chiefs.

culture.label: Bai
culture.text: The men's meeting house, its gables painted with the stories that hold community law.

culture.label: Bul
culture.text: A traditional ban on fishing an area to let it recover — conservation practised for centuries.

culture.label: Diving
culture.text: Consistently rated among the best dive destinations anywhere, and a large part of the economy.

talkAbout: The marine sanctuary and the Palau Pledge.
Diving and the Rock Islands.
The matrilineal system, which surprises most visitors.
avoid: The Compact with the United States and the nuclear question have a long, contested history. Don't take Rock Island souvenirs — collection is restricted.

people.name: Amata Kabua
people.why: The Marshall Islands' first president and the architect of its independence.

people.name: Tony de Brum
people.why: Watched the Bravo test as a child and went on to broker the Paris Agreement's 1.5 °C goal.

people.name: Kathy Jetñil-Kijiner
people.why: Her poem to her daughter opened the 2014 UN climate summit and was heard worldwide.

people.name: Hilda Heine
people.why: The first woman elected head of state of any Pacific island country.

people.name: Darlene Keju
people.why: Told the world about the radiation illnesses the testing programme had caused, and built the country's youth health service.

events.title: Nuclear testing
events.what: The US detonated 67 nuclear weapons at Bikini and Enewetak, displacing whole communities.

events.title: Castle Bravo
events.what: A test a thousand times Hiroshima's yield showered Rongelap with fallout; its people have never fully returned.

events.title: Independence
events.what: The Marshall Islands became sovereign under a Compact of Free Association.

events.title: The Runit Dome
events.what: A concrete lid was poured over radioactive debris on Enewetak; it is cracking as the sea rises.

culture.label: Navigation
culture.text: Marshallese stick charts map ocean swells rather than land — a navigational science found nowhere else.

culture.label: Weaving
culture.text: Pandanus mats and jaki-ed textiles are among the finest weaving in the Pacific.

culture.label: Matrilineal
culture.text: Land rights pass through the mother's line, and women hold considerable authority over it.

culture.label: Kemem
culture.text: A child's first birthday is the biggest party a family will throw, with the whole community fed.

culture.label: Atolls
culture.text: 29 atolls averaging two metres above the sea, spread across nearly two million square kilometres.

talkAbout: Stick charts and traditional navigation.
Weaving, and the patterns particular to each atoll.
Their work at the UN on climate — they are used to being listened to there.
avoid: Nuclear testing is not history here: compensation, displacement and illness are ongoing and were badly handled. Follow their lead on it.

people.name: Hammer DeRoburt
people.why: Led Nauru to independence and negotiated control of its phosphate wealth.

people.name: Marcus Stephen
people.why: Won seven Commonwealth Games golds, then led the country and took its climate case to the UN.

people.name: Baron Waqa
people.why: A teacher and musician who led Nauru and later became Secretary-General of the Pacific Islands Forum.

people.name: Itubwa Amram
people.why: A leading figure in the independence movement and in the Nauruan church.

people.name: Ruben Kun
people.why: A lawyer who pressed Australia at the International Court of Justice over mining damage.

events.title: Phosphate mining begins
events.what: Bird droppings compacted over millennia made Nauru extraordinarily valuable to fertiliser companies.

events.title: Independence
events.what: Nauru became the world's smallest independent republic, at 21 km².

events.title: The richest country per head
events.what: Phosphate royalties briefly gave Nauru one of the highest incomes on earth — then the rock ran out.

events.title: The Pacific Solution
events.what: Nauru began hosting an Australian offshore detention centre, which became a mainstay of its economy and a long-running human rights controversy.

culture.label: Landscape
culture.text: Four-fifths of the island is mined-out limestone pinnacles; almost everyone lives on the coastal strip.

culture.label: Frigatebirds
culture.text: Catching and keeping frigatebirds, then releasing them to return, is a Nauruan tradition.

culture.label: Sport
culture.text: Weightlifting and Australian rules football, both far above what a country of 12,000 should manage.

culture.label: Fishing
culture.text: Noddy-bird catching and reef fishing remain everyday practice.

culture.label: Scale
culture.text: Twelve tribes, one island, 12,000 people — the flag's star marks its position just south of the equator.

talkAbout: Weightlifting and Australian rules football.
The twelve tribes represented on the flag.
Frigatebird catching and other island traditions.
avoid: The detention centre and the exhausted phosphate lands are painful and politically loaded. 'The country that spent it all' is a tired outsider narrative.
